title: Deaf on One Side by Morning
subtitle: A man who woke without hearing in his left ear, from the tuning fork to the audiogram that said he was done
description: Telling sensorineural from conductive at the bedside, what to order and what not to, reading a low-frequency audiogram for what it predicts, treating within the window, keeping the MRI when the hearing improves, and knowing when recovery is complete.

steps.title: Step 1/6: The Tuning Fork
steps.scenario:
A 45-year-old man comes to the clinic at 10 in the morning.

    Complaint       woke this morning unable to hear properly from the left ear
    Ear fullness    yes, left
    Tinnitus        yes, left, a low hum
    Vertigo         none
    Pain            none
    Discharge       none
    Recent illness  none
    Medications     none
    Past history    no ear disease, no previous episode

Otoscopy: both drums normal, no wax, no fluid.

    Weber 512 Hz    lateralizes to the right
    Rinne           air louder than bone, both ears
steps.question: What do the tuning forks tell you?

options.text: (A) The right ear is the problem, because that is where the Weber goes
(B) A conductive loss on the left, probably wax or fluid you have missed
(C) A sensorineural loss on the left: the Weber goes to the better ear and the Rinne is normal on both sides
(D) Nothing reliable; tuning forks cannot localize a hearing loss

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: C

With a normal drum, the first decision is the one the guideline puts first: sensorineural or conductive? The forks answer it in a minute. • Weber lateralizes to the better cochlea in a sensorineural loss, or to the blocked ear in a conductive loss • Rinne stays air-better-than-bone in a sensorineural loss and reverses only with a conductive block. His Weber goes right, his right ear is fine, and his Rinne is normal on both sides: a sudden sensorineural loss on the left. The clock is now running, because the treatment window is short.

(A) The commonest error with the Weber. Sound goes to the better ear in a sensorineural loss. The right ear is where he hears the fork, not where the problem is.
(B) A conductive loss would send the Weber to the left and reverse the Rinne on the left. Neither happened, and the drum is normal.
(D) The forks are exactly the tool for the sensorineural-versus-conductive question, and the guideline's first statement is to make that distinction at presentation.

keypoint: Normal drum, Weber to the good ear, Rinne normal: sudden sensorineural loss, and the clock is running.

Reference:
Chandrasekhar SS, Tsai Do BS, Schwartz SR, et al. Clinical Practice Guideline: Sudden Hearing Loss (Update). Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2019;161(1_suppl):S1-S45. Key Action Statement 1.
2026 note: the 2019 update replaced the 2012 original and remains the current published AAO-HNSF sudden hearing loss CPG.

steps.title: Step 2/6: What to Order Today
steps.scenario:
Sensorineural loss on the left, sudden, this morning. No vertigo, no facial weakness, no other neurological symptom. Right ear normal. First episode.

He asks what tests he needs.
steps.question: What do you order today, and what do you not?

options.text: (A) A pure-tone audiogram today; no CT, no routine blood tests
(B) A CT of the head to exclude a stroke, then the audiogram
(C) A full blood panel, including lipids, glucose, syphilis and autoimmune serology, before any treatment
(D) Nothing today; review in two weeks, since most sudden losses recover on their own

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

The audiogram makes the diagnosis and starts the clock. Sudden sensorineural hearing loss is a loss of at least 30 dB at three consecutive frequencies developing within 72 hours, and the guideline asks for the audiogram within 14 days of onset. Get it today: it confirms the loss, measures it, sets the baseline every later audiogram is compared with, and shapes the prognosis conversation. Two things the guideline says not to do: • no CT of the head, which does not show the cochlea or nerve and delays treatment • no routine laboratory tests in an otherwise well patient with a first unilateral loss. Before leaving the room, check the modifying factors that would change the pathway: bilateral, recurrent, vertigo, focal neurological sign. He has none.

(B) An isolated sudden hearing loss with no vertigo and no neurological sign is not a stroke presentation, and CT is the wrong test for the posterior fossa anyway. The guideline recommends against CT in the initial evaluation.
(C) Routine serology and metabolic screens do not change management in a first, unilateral, uncomplicated loss. Targeted tests are for a history that points somewhere.
(D) Some do recover on their own, but the ones treated within two weeks do better, and you cannot tell in advance which he will be. Waiting two weeks spends the window.

keypoint: Audiogram today; no CT, no routine bloods; ask about the other ear, previous episodes and neurological symptoms.

Reference:
Chandrasekhar SS, Tsai Do BS, Schwartz SR, et al. Clinical Practice Guideline: Sudden Hearing Loss (Update). Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2019;161(1_suppl):S1-S45. Key Action Statements 2, 3, 4 and 5.

steps.title: Step 3/6: Reading the Audiogram
steps.scenario:
Audiogram, same day.

    Right    AC PTA 15 dB, BC PTA 12 dB, SII 98 percent
    Left     AC PTA 49 dB, BC PTA 40 dB, SII 27 percent

    Left air thresholds
    250 Hz   65      2 kHz   40
    500 Hz   65      4 kHz   25
    1 kHz    65      8 kHz   20

    Left bone conduction tracks air conduction at every frequency.
    Speech reception threshold, left    45 dB
steps.media: Load image: Pure-tone audiogram, same day, de-identified
steps.question: How do you characterize this loss, and what does its shape tell you?

options.text: (A) A flat sensorineural loss of about 50 dB; the shape carries no prognostic information
(B) A low-frequency, upsloping sensorineural loss meeting sudden hearing loss criteria; the configuration with the most favorable prognosis, and one that raises the question of cochlear hydrops
(C) A mixed loss: the 9 dB difference between air and bone averages shows a conductive component that needs tympanometry before steroids
(D) A high-frequency loss consistent with noise exposure; not a sudden loss, so there is no treatment window

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: B

The criteria are met: 250, 500 and 1 kHz sit at 65 dB on the left against 5 to 15 dB on the right, a difference of at least 50 dB at three consecutive frequencies. The shape is the point: • low frequencies down to 65 dB • high frequencies near normal at 20 to 25 dB • a 40 dB tilt from 1 to 4 kHz. This is an upsloping, low-frequency configuration, which the guideline's counseling statement identifies as the pattern with the best chance of recovery, in contrast to profound or downsloping losses. Low-tone loss with fullness is also the phenotype of cochlear hydrops. A first episode is managed as sudden sensorineural loss; the labels of acute low-tone hearing loss or Meniere's disease are applied in retrospect, and in a scoping review of 41 studies the majority of such patients recovered, recurrence was common, and progression to Meniere's disease was infrequent.

(A) Not flat. Sixty-five at the low frequencies and 20 at 8 kHz is a 45 dB difference across the audiogram, and configuration is one of the prognostic factors the guideline asks you to counsel on.
(C) Nine dB between air and bone averages is within test-retest variability, the bone thresholds track air at every frequency, the drum is normal and the Rinne is positive. There is no conductive component to chase, and chasing it delays treatment.
(D) The reverse of what is on the page. High-frequency thresholds are the best part of this audiogram.

keypoint: Read the shape, not just the average. A low-frequency loss recovers best, and it is the pattern that can turn out to be hydrops.

Reference:
Chandrasekhar SS, Tsai Do BS, Schwartz SR, et al. Clinical Practice Guideline: Sudden Hearing Loss (Update). Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2019;161(1_suppl):S1-S45. Key Action Statements 4 and 7.
Huang RJ, Del Risco A, Riska KM, Cooper MW, Clark NW, Kaplan SJ, Kaylie D, Francis HW. Prognosis of Acute Low-Tone Hearing Loss Without Vertigo: A Scoping Review. Laryngoscope. 2023;133(10):2457-2469.

steps.title: Step 4/6: The Window
steps.scenario:
Sudden sensorineural hearing loss confirmed, left, low-frequency configuration. Onset this morning. He is otherwise well, not diabetic, no contraindication to steroids.

He asks what treatment he should have.
steps.question: What treatment do you offer, and by when?

options.text: (A) A diuretic and salt restriction alone, since a low-frequency loss with fullness is hydrops rather than a sudden sensorineural loss
(B) No treatment; low-frequency losses usually recover on their own, so observe for two weeks
(C) A course of corticosteroid started now, oral or intratympanic, within two weeks of onset, after explaining what it can and cannot do
(D) Admission for high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone, because a larger dose gives a larger effect

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: C

Corticosteroids are the only initial treatment with evidence behind them, and the evidence is time-dependent: benefit is seen when treatment starts within two weeks of onset and fades after that. The guideline grades this as an option, because some patients recover untreated and the decision belongs to a patient who has heard the numbers, so the conversation and the offer happen today. Two routes, equally supported as first-line: • oral prednisolone or prednisone, about 1 mg/kg/day to 60 mg, for 7 to 14 days then taper • intratympanic dexamethasone, which a randomized comparison and a Cochrane review found equivalent as primary therapy and which suits anyone who should avoid systemic exposure. Hyperbaric oxygen with steroids is a further option within two weeks where available.

(A) Some centers add a diuretic for the low-tone phenotype, but the evidence is heterogeneous, the guideline does not endorse it, and it is not a substitute for steroids in a first episode that meets sudden hearing loss criteria. The label of hydrops is retrospective; the treatment window is not.
(B) The favorable configuration improves the odds; it does not remove the window. Observation is legitimate if he declines steroids after counseling, not a way of deciding whether to offer them.
(D) The HODOKORT trial randomized more than 300 patients to standard oral dosing versus high-dose systemic regimens and found no better hearing with the higher dose, with more adverse events and worse speech recognition and tinnitus outcomes. More is not better.

keypoint: Offer steroids within two weeks, oral or intratympanic, after the patient has heard what they can and cannot do. Megadoses add nothing; diuretics are not a substitute.

Reference:
Chandrasekhar SS, Tsai Do BS, Schwartz SR, et al. Clinical Practice Guideline: Sudden Hearing Loss (Update). Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2019;161(1_suppl):S1-S45. Key Action Statements 7, 8, 9a and 11.
Rauch SD, Halpin CF, Antonelli PJ, et al. Oral vs intratympanic corticosteroid therapy for idiopathic sudden sensorineural hearing loss: a randomized trial. JAMA. 2011;305(20):2071-2079.
Plontke SK, Meisner C, Agrawal S, et al. Intratympanic corticosteroids for sudden sensorineural hearing loss. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2022;7:CD008080.
Plontke SK, Girndt M, Meisner C, et al. High-Dose Glucocorticoids for the Treatment of Sudden Hearing Loss. NEJM Evid. 2024;3(1). doi:10.1056/EVIDoa2300172.

steps.title: Step 5/6: Three Days Later
steps.scenario:
He started oral prednisolone the same day. Three days later he returns for a repeat audiogram.

    Left     AC PTA 34 dB, improved from 49
             SII 59 percent, improved from 27
    Right    unchanged

He says the fullness is easing and asks whether the MRI you mentioned is still necessary, since he is clearly getting better.
steps.media: Load image: Pure-tone audiogram, three days after onset, de-identified
steps.question: Does he still need imaging?

options.text: (A) No; improvement this early on steroids makes a retrocochlear lesion very unlikely
(B) Yes: MRI of the internal auditory canals and brain with gadolinium, regardless of how the hearing behaves
(C) Repeat the audiogram at two weeks and image only if recovery stalls
(D) CT of the temporal bones, which is faster and cheaper, since he is improving anyway

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: B

Most sudden sensorineural losses are idiopathic, but a few are the first sign of something on the nerve: a vestibular schwannoma, a meningioma, a demyelinating plaque, a small stroke in the anterior inferior cerebellar artery territory. The proportion is small but not zero, and a tumor is treatable if found. The guideline recommends evaluating every patient with sudden sensorineural loss for retrocochlear pathology, and the test is MRI of the internal auditory canals and brain with gadolinium; auditory brainstem response is the fallback for a patient who cannot have MRI. Two things about timing: • the MRI is not an emergency and does not delay treatment; it is ordered at the first visit and done in the following weeks • recovery does not exclude a tumor.

(A) The premature-reassurance trap. Schwannomas present with sudden loss that partly or fully recovers, with or without steroids, often enough that improvement cannot be used to skip the scan. Improvement is reassuring for the cochlea, not for the nerve.
(C) Waiting for recovery to stall inverts the logic. The recommendation is to image after the first event, because a first event is how most schwannomas with sudden loss present.
(D) CT shows bone. A schwannoma is soft tissue in the canal and the cerebellopontine angle, and CT misses small ones entirely. The guideline recommends against CT for this question.

keypoint: Every sudden sensorineural loss gets an MRI of the internal auditory canals with contrast, whether or not the hearing comes back.

Reference:
Chandrasekhar SS, Tsai Do BS, Schwartz SR, et al. Clinical Practice Guideline: Sudden Hearing Loss (Update). Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2019;161(1_suppl):S1-S45. Key Action Statement 6.

steps.title: Step 6/6: One Week Later
steps.scenario:
One week after onset. He is on the tail of the prednisolone taper. Fullness gone, tinnitus faded.

    Left     AC PTA 22 dB, SII 93 percent
    Right    AC PTA 18 dB, SII 96 percent

    Left air thresholds now 30, 25, 25, 20, 20, 15 dB from 250 Hz to 8 kHz.

He asks whether he is cured, and whether he can stop the tablets and forget about the scan.
steps.media: Load image: Pure-tone audiogram, one week after onset, de-identified
steps.question: How do you classify this outcome, and what do you do now?

options.text: (A) Complete recovery. Finish the taper, keep the MRI, arrange a follow-up audiogram with a measured word recognition score within six months, and counsel him about recurrence
(B) Partial recovery, because a 22 dB average is still outside the normal range; offer intratympanic salvage now
(C) Complete recovery, so stop the steroid today, cancel the MRI, and discharge
(D) Complete recovery, but the low-frequency pattern means this was Meniere's disease, so start a diuretic and salt restriction to prevent the next attack

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

The guideline asks that outcomes be reported against the patient's own other ear, not against a population norm: complete recovery is a pure-tone average within 10 dB of the unaffected ear with speech scores back to that ear's level. He is at 22 dB against 18, and his low frequencies have risen from 65 to 25 to 30 dB. That is complete recovery by definition, and it happened in a week, which is what a low-frequency configuration treated on day one often does. Three things still need doing: • finish the taper rather than stopping abruptly • keep the MRI, for the reason in Step 5 • a follow-up audiogram within six months, which is the guideline's outcome-assessment statement, and it should include a measured word recognition score, because the SII on this report is calculated from the thresholds rather than measured. Then counsel: with this phenotype, recurrence and fluctuation are common even though progression to Meniere's disease is infrequent, so any new fullness, fluctuation or vertigo should bring him back.

(B) Twenty-two dB is within 10 dB of his own right ear at 18, and the guideline's yardstick is the other ear, not the 20 dB population line. Intratympanic salvage is for incomplete recovery, and there is nothing to salvage.
(C) Two of the three are wrong. Steroid courses are tapered, and the MRI is indicated by the event, not by the outcome. Discharge without a follow-up audiogram also skips a recommendation.
(D) The premature-labeling trap. Meniere's disease requires at least two spontaneous vertigo attacks lasting 20 minutes to 12 hours, with documented low-to-mid-frequency loss and fluctuating aural symptoms. He has never had vertigo and has had one episode. A low-tone loss that recovers is a risk marker worth naming to him, not a diagnosis to treat.

keypoint: Judge recovery against the other ear, not the normal range; complete recovery does not cancel the MRI or the follow-up; one episode is not Meniere's.

Reference:
Chandrasekhar SS, Tsai Do BS, Schwartz SR, et al. Clinical Practice Guideline: Sudden Hearing Loss (Update). Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2019;161(1_suppl):S1-S45. Key Action Statements 6 and 12.
Huang RJ, Del Risco A, Riska KM, Cooper MW, Clark NW, Kaplan SJ, Kaylie D, Francis HW. Prognosis of Acute Low-Tone Hearing Loss Without Vertigo: A Scoping Review. Laryngoscope. 2023;133(10):2457-2469.
Basura GJ, Adams ME, Monfared A, et al. Clinical Practice Guideline: Meniere's Disease. Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2020;162(2_suppl):S1-S55.
